title: Perplexity and Intelligence
author: OpenAI News
contentSnippet:
November 22, 2026 Research Safety Perplexity and Intelligence By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models th

summary.tldr:
Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI, argues that perplexity (cross-entropy loss) should serve as the industry-standard metric for tracking AI progress and establishing shared safety benchmarks. Pachocki posits that modern AI development is fundamentally the process of training a compressor on massive datasets, where lower perplexity consistently correlates with the emergence of transformative, latent capabilities. By publishing OpenAI’s internal perplexity trajectory, he aims to foster industry-wide transparency and encourage developers to agree on common development limits based on these metrics until monitoring capabilities, such as successors to chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors, reach sufficient maturity.

OpenAI’s internal data shows a clear correlation between decreasing log-perplexity and model capability leaps: GPT-3.5 reached ~0.99, GPT-4 hit ~0.91, and current models have surpassed 0.8. Pachocki highlights that models reaching ~0.76 log-perplexity have demonstrated the ability to solve groundbreaking mathematical problems. He projects that the next major capability threshold will likely emerge within the 0.68–0.7 log-perplexity window. While acknowledging that perplexity does not capture all advancements—notably excluding CoT reasoning gains—he argues it remains the most reliable "intelligence substrate" metric for predicting the emergence of new, potentially dangerous capabilities as AI begins to accelerate its own algorithmic research.
takeaways: **Performance Benchmarks:** OpenAI models have progressed from GPT-3.5 (~0.99 log-perplexity) and GPT-4 (~0.91) to current models below 0.8, with a significant breakthrough in mathematical reasoning observed at ~0.76.
**Future Projections:** Pachocki anticipates a new wave of transformative capabilities as models reach the 0.68–0.7 log-perplexity range, potentially as early as 2027.

**Proposed Safety Framework:** OpenAI advocates for an industry-wide standard that sets concrete development limits based on perplexity, requiring specific monitoring milestones (e.g., advanced CoT monitors) before proceeding to lower loss thresholds.

**Metric Limitations:** Perplexity does not account for non-pretraining gains like chain-of-thought reasoning, and cross-lab comparisons remain difficult due to disparate evaluation datasets and training mixtures.

title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values
author: Yichen Zhao, Fenghe Tang, Wenxin Ma, Rongsheng Wang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yichen Zhao , Fenghe Tang , Wenxin Ma , Rongsheng Wang , Zihao Wan , Shaohua Kevin Zhou

Abstract: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at this https URL .

summary.tldr:
Researchers Yichen Zhao, Fenghe Tang, Wenxin Ma, Rongsheng Wang, Zihao Wan, and Shaohua Kevin Zhou have introduced VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), a method designed to improve medical Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by focusing on visual values rather than spatial attention maps. The study challenges the prevailing assumption that attention maps are the primary indicator of effective visual perception, demonstrating that MLLMs often produce identical attention patterns for non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images despite the images providing different diagnostic cues.

To address this, the authors developed a medical VQA dataset containing paired NC and CE images. Their experiments revealed that bidirectional interventions on visual values result in significantly larger prediction changes than interventions on attention weights. VIVID leverages this insight by using enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections, facilitating on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. The method allows models to achieve superior performance using only NC images at inference time, outperforming existing on-policy distillation techniques across six internal and external test sets while maintaining zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation) shifts focus from spatial attention maps to visual values to improve medical image perception.
**Experimental Dataset:** The study utilizes a custom medical VQA dataset consisting of paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images.
**Performance:** VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across various model scales and architectures.
**Inference Efficiency:** The proposed method requires only NC images during inference while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy.
**Generalization:** The approach preserves strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks.

title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
author: Wenyi Wu, Siqi Liu, Yuru Feng, Zixuan Song
contentSnippet:
Authors: Wenyi Wu , Siqi Liu , Yuru Feng , Zixuan Song , Aayush Salvi , Sibo Zhu , Kun Zhou , Biwei Huang

Abstract: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

summary.tldr:
GameAnything is an open-source agentic platform designed to convert multimodal inspirations—such as images, text, or videos—into playable game extensions. Developed by a research team including Wenyi Wu, Siqi Liu, and others, the system utilizes a multi-component architecture featuring coding agents, an independent playtesting critic, a persistent development state, and a reusable experience memory. This framework enables iterative refinement of game code, allowing the system to adapt existing game environments based on user-provided references.

To evaluate the platform, the researchers introduced GameAnything-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark covering various reference modalities, development objectives, and gaming environments. The benchmark assesses both functional code correctness and the quality of the resulting gameplay experience. Testing across nine different coding agent configurations demonstrated that while agents can successfully incorporate reference content, they currently face significant limitations in executing precise modifications and ensuring robust, playable interactions. The study concludes that while iterative refinement and multimodal inputs improve content fidelity, achieving high-quality, inspiration-driven game development remains a significant technical challenge.
takeaways: **Platform Architecture:** GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic and a persistent development state to facilitate iterative game creation.
**Benchmark Scope:** GameAnything-Bench evaluates performance across diverse reference modalities, specific game creation objectives, and multiple gaming environments.

**Performance Findings:** Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations show that current models struggle with precise modifications and playable interactions despite improvements in content fidelity.
**Iterative Impact:** The research confirms that iterative refinement processes yield substantial but inconsistent improvements across different agent configurations.

title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
author: Meng-Hao Guo, Yi Zhang, Zhe-Han Mo, Han-Zheng Wang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Meng-Hao Guo , Yi Zhang , Zhe-Han Mo , Han-Zheng Wang , Jia-Jun Wang , Xin-Sheng Chen , Jiaxi Song , Yi-Xuan Deng , Jia-Ning Li , Xuanyu Chu , Hengrui Zhang , Huan-ang Gao , Yongming Rao , Shi-Min Hu

Abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Meng-Hao Guo et al. have introduced nanoAstra, a vision-language model (VLM) framework designed to replicate the generalization capabilities of GPT-6 Astra for robotic manipulation. The approach centers on two primary innovations: semantic action modeling, which decomposes robot behavior into reusable, parameterized action primitives guided by progress descriptions, and capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). CP-SFT utilizes a robot-specific system prompt to constrain outputs to a structured action space, allowing the model to adapt to specific robotic contexts while preserving its broader pretrained knowledge base.

The model was trained on a dataset comprising over 5,000 hours of robotic data integrated with general visual question answering (VQA) data. In testing on the RoboTwin 2.0 randomized benchmark, the 9-billion parameter nanoAstra-9B model achieved a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, outperforming existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World-Action Model (WAM) baselines. Beyond success rates, the architecture optimizes operational efficiency; by enabling action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps model inference with physical motion on a single H20 GPU, the system reduced robot idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** nanoAstra-9B utilizes semantic action modeling to map robot behavior to parameterized primitives.
**Training Data:** The model was trained on a combined dataset of over 5,000 hours of robot-specific data and general VQA data.
**Performance Metric:** On the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieved a 17.8% zero-shot success rate.
**Efficiency Gains:** Streaming execution enabled by the model reduced robot idle time from 35.0% to 6.9% on H20 hardware.

title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification
author: Seifeldin Elkerdany, Mohamed ElBassat, Gamal Abouelhamd, Assem Elkady
contentSnippet:
Authors: Seifeldin Elkerdany , Mohamed ElBassat , Gamal Abouelhamd , Assem Elkady , Jana Ghoneim , Matin Mahmood , Abigail Allen Martin , Gerard de Melo , Antonio Rueda-Toicen

Abstract: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.

title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
author: Panagiotis Kasnesis, Lazaros Toumanidis, Amalia Contiero Syropoulou, Christos Chatzigeorgiou
contentSnippet: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.

title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
author: Shuaiwei Huang, Weihua Du, Allen Wu, Ivan Fox
contentSnippet: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

title: Muru
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture , he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too. Tags: graham-dumpleton , modwsgi , python , wsgi , ai , rust , asgi , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-programming

summary.tldr:
Graham Dumpleton, the creator of mod_wsgi, has introduced Muru, an AI-assisted server written in Rust designed to serve both ASGI and WSGI Python applications in production and development environments. Drawing on two decades of experience with mod_wsgi, Dumpleton is developing Muru with a heavy reliance on AI-assisted programming, documenting the process through a series of technical deep dives published between November 4 and November 21, 2026.

Muru’s architecture focuses on modern deployment paradigms, specifically targeting containerized environments and Kubernetes integration. Key technical features detailed in the project documentation include an 'import once, fork many' execution model, native HTTPS support for development, and built-in canary deployment capabilities that function without the need for a traditional service mesh. The server also implements advanced operational features such as scaling to zero, scheduled overlays, and a diagnostic toolbar that provides real-time tracing directly on served pages.

Dumpleton emphasizes that while AI accelerates the development of Muru, his long-term experience in Python web server architecture remains the primary filter for quality and reliability. The project aims to provide a robust, production-ready alternative to existing Python application servers by addressing common pain points in container orchestration and application lifecycle management.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** Muru is a Rust-based server supporting both ASGI and WSGI standards, designed to optimize Python application performance in production.
**Kubernetes Integration:** The server is built to operate natively within Kubernetes, featuring scaling-to-zero capabilities and worker-reported scaling metrics.
**Operational Features:** Includes built-in canary deployment support, HTTPS for development, and a diagnostic toolbar for in-page tracing.

**Development Methodology:** The project is being developed using AI-assisted coding, with Dumpleton publishing daily technical logs detailing the implementation of specific features like process management and container tenancy.

title: Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief
author: Sloane Kali Faye
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 16:48 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026

Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”

Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26 , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.)

Building a sovereign AI factory without lock-in

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller said. “We have to look for the data.”

summary.tldr:
The HammerHAI AI factory in Stuttgart, led by managing director Bastian Koller of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart, is deploying a new supercomputing infrastructure based on Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) systems utilizing Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs. The facility aims to provide European startups and small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs) with high-performance computing resources while prioritizing data sovereignty and avoiding vendor lock-in. Rather than pursuing full hardware independence, the center focuses on data control and portability, ensuring that workloads can be migrated between the facility and commercial hyperscalers.

Technically, the new system represents a significant efficiency upgrade, doubling the performance of its predecessor while reducing power consumption from 3.2 megawatts to approximately 700 kilowatts, with additional waste heat recovery. The center operates under ISO-certified standards and maintains TISAX Level 3 certification to support automotive industry requirements. To bridge the gap between complex infrastructure and user needs, the facility employs a 'concierge model' that assigns dedicated contacts to customers, ensuring that the system architecture is informed by real-world user workflows rather than purely theoretical design.
takeaways: **Hardware Architecture:** The HammerHAI facility is built on HPE systems powered by Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips.
**Energy Efficiency:** The new system delivers double the performance of the previous 3.2-megawatt infrastructure while operating at a 700-kilowatt power draw.
**Compliance Standards:** The facility maintains ISO certification and TISAX Level 3 certification, specifically to accommodate automotive sector data security requirements.
**Operational Model:** The center utilizes a concierge service model to provide hands-on support for SMEs and startups, prioritizing workload portability to prevent vendor lock-in.

title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
author: Anthony Ha
contentSnippet: Posted: 1:37 PM PST · November 21, 2026 Image Credits: Matthias Balk/picture alliance / Getty Images Anthony Ha Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance Signal announced Friday that it’s limi

summary.tldr:
Signal has announced new restrictions on mobile screenshots within its messaging application, extending existing Windows-based protections to its Android and iOS platforms. Signal President Meredith Whittaker framed the move as a necessary defense against the "existential threat" posed by OS-level agentic AI, which can scan, capture, and store sensitive user data from the screen, effectively bypassing the app's end-to-end encryption guarantees.

Whittaker noted that when operating systems integrate AI agents capable of monitoring screen content, the data becomes accessible to local databases or remote servers outside of Signal's control. While the new restrictions aim to mitigate this risk, the feature remains optional; users retain the ability to disable the screenshot block, though doing so explicitly compromises the app's privacy model. Whittaker acknowledged that this is an incomplete solution, as it does not address alternative methods by which AI agents might access application data.
takeaways: **Platform Expansion:** Signal is extending its screenshot-blocking feature, previously exclusive to Windows, to its Android and iOS mobile applications.
**Privacy Rationale:** The update is a direct response to OS-level agentic AI capabilities that can capture and exfiltrate screen data, undermining Signal's privacy guarantees.
**User Control:** The screenshot restriction is not mandatory; users can toggle the setting off, though Signal warns this action breaks their privacy protections.
**Technical Limitation:** Signal leadership admits the measure is an "incomplete" defense, as it does not prevent other, more sophisticated methods for AI agents to access in-app data.

title: A tale of two Nvidias
author: Anthony Ha
contentSnippet:
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20

summary.tldr:
Nvidia is currently navigating a dual-narrative crisis involving internal leadership instability and tightening geopolitical export controls. While the company reported strong financial results that exceeded market expectations, it simultaneously faces public pressure from high-profile tech figures, including Elon Musk, who are campaigning for the return of former CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board has officially rejected these calls, maintaining that current leadership is in control, though analysts note the company's public stance has shifted rapidly in recent weeks, fueling speculation about internal board dynamics and potential parallels to the leadership volatility previously seen at OpenAI.

Simultaneously, Nvidia has confirmed it will cease sales of its H200 chips to China. This move aligns with intensifying U.S. government restrictions aimed at closing loopholes that previously allowed Chinese entities to access advanced hardware via remote access from data centers located in third-party countries like Malaysia. Industry observers estimate that approximately 20% of Nvidia’s business may be tied to the Chinese market through these indirect channels, suggesting that a full enforcement of these export controls could significantly impact the company’s long-term revenue, despite current financial guidance remaining robust.
takeaways: **Export Control Policy:** Nvidia has officially halted the sale of H200 chips to China to comply with tightening U.S. restrictions on both direct hardware exports and remote access to compute resources.

**Market Exposure:** Analysts estimate that up to 20% of Nvidia’s total business is indirectly linked to the Chinese market, posing a potential risk to future revenue if current loopholes are fully closed.

**Leadership Conflict:** A public campaign, supported by figures like Elon Musk, is calling for the reinstatement of former CEO Jensen Huang, despite the current board’s explicit denial of such plans.

**Financial Performance:** Despite geopolitical headwinds and leadership drama, Nvidia’s most recent quarterly earnings beat market expectations, with the company maintaining a strong pipeline and positive financial guidance.

title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations. According to NPR: > Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan. According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: > On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

summary.tldr:
UN diplomats meeting in Geneva failed to establish a framework for regulating autonomous weapons, commonly referred to as “killer robots,” instead agreeing only to begin discussing potential options. Despite urgent calls from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the UN secretary-general, and the Pope for legally binding regulations to be drafted within one year, the resulting compromise grants nations a two-year window to propose guidelines. Humanitarian groups argue that immediate, binding rules are essential given the documented civilian casualties caused by semi-autonomous drones and weapons systems in active conflict zones, including Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

The negotiations faced significant procedural and ideological friction, primarily from Russia, the United States, and Israel. Russia initiated delays on the first day by challenging the meeting's agenda, while the United States advocated for a five-year timeline focused on nonbinding, optional guidelines. The final consensus leaves open the possibility that any future regulations may remain voluntary, suggesting that substantive enforcement mechanisms remain unlikely in the near term.
takeaways: **Regulatory Timeline:** Member states have been granted two years to propose regulations, extending beyond the one-year deadline requested by the International Committee of the Red Cross.
**Primary Obstructionists:** Russia, the United States, and Israel were identified as the main countries resisting the implementation of immediate, legally binding rules.
**US Proposal:** The United States pushed for a five-year discussion period centered on nonbinding, optional guidelines rather than a treaty.
**Conflict Context:** Humanitarian concerns are driven by the use of semi-autonomous weapons in ongoing conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

title: Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed
author: Kelly Knight
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 13:28 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026

Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, quickly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26 , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.)

Why modular data centers suit low-power inference

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill said. “We went with commodity memory.”

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap

summary.tldr:
AI hardware spending has inverted from training dominance to inference-first workloads, according to Cameron McCaskill, head of sales and business development at Positron AI Inc., speaking at SC26. While infrastructure was 85% training and 15% inference in 2023, inference now accounts for two-thirds of workloads. This shift is driving capital toward smaller, modular data centers where power, cooling, and memory supply dictate token generation sites rather than giant training clusters.

To capitalize on this shift, Positron AI—which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September—builds inference appliances utilizing commodity memory instead of scarce and expensive high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Positron's first-generation Atlas server uses a programmable chip, with Oracle bringing roughly 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud during the quarter. The company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its upcoming Titan server, which has already secured a commitment from a neocloud provider.

By avoiding HBM, Positron maintains a low power profile suitable for air-cooled environments: a single server draws roughly 4,500 watts, and a full Titan rack operates within 40 kilowatts. This thermal and electrical footprint allows operators to deploy in half-megawatt to 2.5-megawatt modular data centers, targeting a timeline of 90 to 120 days from land and power acquisition to monetizing tokens.
takeaways: **Workload Shift:** Inference workloads have grown from 15% in 2023 to two-thirds of total AI infrastructure workloads, overtaking training as the primary driver of infrastructure buying decisions.
**Funding and Valuation:** Positron AI Inc. raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September.
**Memory Architecture:** Positron uses commodity memory instead of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to avoid supply scarcity and high costs.

**Hardware Roadmap:** Positron's first-generation Atlas server runs on a programmable chip (with ~340 units going live in Oracle's cloud this quarter), while custom silicon for the upcoming Titan server is scheduled for tape-out early next year.

**Power and Deployment Footprint:** Individual Positron servers draw about 4,500 watts, a full Titan rack fits within 40 kilowatts, and the low-power design allows modular data center deployment in 90 to 120 days.

title: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement
author: David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 12:50 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026

Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement .

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:

First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide , which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26 , which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Why a sovereign AI framework is needed

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:

In-depth interviews rev

summary.tldr:
Breaking Analysis #334, authored by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin, and John Furrier, establishes a framework for 'Sovereign AI' as an architectural requirement for global firms in regulated industries. The analysis, supported by a survey of 11 senior technology decision-makers and a proprietary buyer’s guide, highlights a significant gap between buyer concerns regarding jurisdictional risk and their actual operational testing. Most organizations currently rely on existing cloud providers rather than dedicated sovereign offerings, citing cost and the burden of managing additional environments as primary barriers. The report emphasizes that sovereignty is not a binary 'purity test' but a risk-management exercise requiring deliberate decisions regarding data residency, key management, and support protocols.

The analysis introduces a sovereign cloud scoring index based on five pillars: territorial, legal, operational, technical, and financial. Google leads the index with a score of 3.45, followed by Oracle (3.25), IBM and Microsoft Azure (3.0), and AWS (2.7). Huawei and Alibaba scored 1.2. The report notes that AWS’s lower score is attributed to the lack of a customer-run, air-gapped stack option. Crucially, the authors warn that technical controls are insufficient to mitigate risks posed by the U.S. CLOUD Act, which can compel vendors under U.S. jurisdiction to produce data regardless of physical storage location. Buyers are advised to treat sovereign exposure as a cybersecurity-level assessment, balancing model capability against jurisdictional risk for specific workloads.
takeaways: **Sovereign Cloud Scoring:** Google leads the vendor index at 3.45, followed by Oracle (3.25), IBM and Microsoft (3.0), AWS (2.7), and Huawei/Alibaba (1.2).
**Operational Gaps:** 7 of 11 surveyed decision-makers reported no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation, or exit scenarios, despite high concerns over jurisdictional control.

**Inference Trade-offs:** 9 of 11 respondents require AI inference to occur within sovereign boundaries, often forcing a trade-off between local compliance and access to the latest model capabilities.
**Legal Limitations:** The U.S. CLOUD Act remains a primary 'gotcha,' as locally incorporated subsidiaries or customer-held keys do not guarantee legal immunity from U.S. data production requests.
**Support Protocol Risk:** Even in sovereign deployments, deep technical support escalations may involve personnel or systems outside the local jurisdiction, requiring explicit architectural review.

title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
author: Lauren Forristal
contentSnippet:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September

A growing ecosystem of AI personal assistants is emerging directly within text-messaging platforms like iMessage, RCS, WhatsApp, and Telegram, bypassing standalone app downloads. Leading this space is Instinct, valued at $10 billion following a $1 billion funding round, alongside newer entrants like Tab, which emerged from stealth in October 2026 with a $300 million valuation backed by SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

These messaging-native agents span diverse use cases, from general productivity to specialized family management, content creation, and professional workflows. Specific offerings include Caddy (public beta since April 2026), Fambot (family chief of staff with $3.5 million pre-seed funding, pricing planned around a Netflix subscription), Haven (digital twin via app, web, or phone call/text), Iris (powered by Hermes Agent), Maverick (free on iMessage with a €27/month Pro tier for 500 tasks and 20 connected apps), Ohai (family tiers starting at $9.99/month), Pally, Rene (capable of browsing, coding, and slide/image creation), Stanley (content creator assistant connected to Instagram), Town ($55 million Series A in June 2026 led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner), and Wajo's Fo (equipped with its own email, phone number, payment card, and human-in-the-loop fallback).

**Tab Funding & Launch:** Emerged from stealth in early October 2026 with a $300 million valuation backed by SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.
**Town Series A:** Raised $55 million in June 2026 in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner for its professional-focused 'Townie' assistant.
**Fambot Metrics:** Raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding after launching a beta in early September 2026, with planned subscription pricing equivalent to a Netflix subscription.
**Maverick Pricing:** Offers a free beta tier on iMessage alongside a Pro version priced at €27 per month (approx. $30.25 USD) for 500 monthly tasks and 20 connected apps.

title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”

Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.

Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.

This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”

Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mob

summary.tldr:
Microdrama startup Shortical, founded in January, is shifting its production focus toward AI-generated content to lower overhead costs and increase profit potential compared to traditional live-action series. The company recently premiered a fully AI-generated series titled "Inevitable" in Los Angeles, starring Israeli actor Aki Avni via a direct licensing deal for his digital avatar, making him a pioneer in Hollywood face-licensing for AI media.

Shortical operates primarily on a subscription model, offering the first 7 to 10 episodes of soapy, melodramatic romances free before requiring a monthly fee to unlock full series like "Accidentally Married My Boss" and "Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy." CEO Guy Shimoni states that AI tools allow smaller teams to produce high-cost settings like kingdoms, dragons, and werewolves that were previously restricted by live-action budgets. While the microdrama genre originated in China—where face-licensing deals range from $15 to $700—Shortical is now actively soliciting U.S. creators to license their facial likenesses by submitting social media handles, partnering with Payouts.com to handle creator disbursements.

The push toward automation has sparked widespread industry backlash and distrust. Jennifer Cooper, founder of consultancy Vertical Drama Love, notes that AI has devastated entry-level acting opportunities and that venture capitalists demand AI integration for funding. While Shortical compensated Avni in line with industry standards as a project partner, the company has declined to specify exact financial terms for future creators or whether it will offer recurring residuals, leaving the long-term economic model for gig-ified face licensing uncertain.
takeaways: **Startup Launch and Business Model:** Founded last January, Shortical produces 2-minute episodic microdramas monetized via monthly subscriptions after an initial free window of 7 to 10 episodes.

**First AI-Avatar Series:** The Los Angeles premiere of "Inevitable" marks Shortical's first project featuring a real actor's digital avatar, utilizing a direct likeness agreement with Israeli actor Aki Avni.
**Creator Likeness Solicitations:** Shortical is actively inviting creators to submit social media handles via its website to negotiate face-licensing contracts for automated content generation.
**Gig-Economy Infrastructure:** Shortical partnered with Payouts.com to build a payment infrastructure capable of managing disbursements for creators and gig workers at scale.

**Industry Backlash and VC Pressure:** Industry experts note that venture capitalists demand AI integration for funding, while traditional creatives criticize the automation for eliminating entry-level acting work and raising consent concerns.

title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
author: Nilay Patel

The conversation focuses on the tension between Anthropic's stated commitment to AI safety and its new status as a public company beholden to shareholders, particularly as it faces escalating compute bills projected at roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

title: Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android. “Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.” Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and so

summary.tldr:
Chess.com is expanding its platform beyond chess with the launch of "Classic Games," a new hub featuring 10 additional titles: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble-like game titled "word." The platform, which follows the earlier launch of the gambling-free poker site Gambit, will enter public beta this Saturday via web, iOS, and Android. According to Chief Growth Officer Albert Cheng, the expansion aims to provide a centralized community for classic games that currently lack the infrastructure and social features Chess.com has built for its nearly 300 million members.

The Classic Games platform leverages the existing Chess.com codebase, design system, and established rating and bot infrastructure. Development was accelerated by using AI for coding tasks, a strategy previously employed for the Gambit launch, allowing a small team to deploy 11 games in a matter of months. Despite the use of AI for engineering, Cheng emphasized that all art and design assets are human-crafted. The new games include features consistent with the core site, such as lessons, leaderboards, and bot-based play, with specific modes like daily grids for sudoku and daily deals for solitaire.
takeaways: **Platform Expansion:** Chess.com is adding 10 classic games to its ecosystem, including strategy titles like shogi and xiangqi, and casual games like solitaire and sudoku.
**Development Methodology:** The company utilized AI to accelerate coding and infrastructure integration, while maintaining human-led design and art production.
**Infrastructure Reuse:** New games are built on the existing Chess.com framework, allowing for shared features like the rating system, bot characters, and lesson modules.
**Resource Allocation:** Less than 1% of the company's total workforce is currently dedicated to building these new game titles, keeping the primary focus on the core chess platform.
**User Growth:** Chess.com reports that its daily active user count is currently at an all-time high.

title: Meet Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Mini: 26B Looped MoE Runs on a 32GB Mac
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini , an open-weight looped transformer with 26.4B total parameters. The model reuses its middle layers 3 times per token instead of adding more weights. That keeps the checkpoint near 20GB, small enough for a 32GB Mac or 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark. For developers, Inkling 2 Mini is a local option for agentic coding, tool use and document work. It ships under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face , with hosted inference and fine-tuning on Tinker . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 26.4B total, 3.4B active (5.4B effective per token with looping), up to 1M-token context. Runs on: Apple silicon with 32GB+ memory, 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark, or GPUs with 32GB+ VRAM. GGUF builds via Unsloth and llama.cpp. Performance: 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Index, tied with Qwen3.8-27B (self-reported). Best: 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only). Worst: 15.2% on HLE-Diamond and 50.0% on MultiChallenge. Bottom line: Best: strong agentic coding from a 20GB checkpoint. Worst: weaker knowledge recall and multi-turn instruction following. What is Inkling 2 Mini? Inkling 2 Mini is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from Thinking Machines that loops its middle layers. It accepts text and images and returns text only. It follows Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter model released on November 5. How does the looped transformer work? The model stores 24 layers, grouped into 4 blocks of 6. The first and last blocks run once. The 2 middle blocks run 3 times with shared weights. That gives 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. Each pass after the first receives a “message” from the previous pass. Thinking Machines carries it with Attention Residuals and a learned gate. Feed-forward layers use 128 experts, with 8 routed per token. Looping the middle layers gave a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain. Looping the last layers gave only 1.24x to 1.36x. The middle-loop variant won 27 of 28 evaluations. Looping costs training compute but saves inference. An unlooped baseline used 7.5% less training compute. It needed 140% more inference compute to match the looped model’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces. How was Inkling 2 Mini trained? Training began with 384 experts per layer, with 8 active per token. At midtraining, the team pruned two-thirds of them and kept the 128

summary.tldr:
Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that utilizes a looped transformer architecture to achieve high performance with a 20GB checkpoint. By reusing its middle layers three times per token, the model effectively simulates 48 layer applications from only 24 physical layers. This design allows the model to run on consumer hardware, specifically Apple silicon with 32GB of RAM or a single NVIDIA DGX Spark, while supporting a context window of up to 1 million tokens. The model is released under an Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face, with fine-tuning and inference support available via the Tinker platform.

Technically, the model architecture consists of 24 layers grouped into four blocks of six, where the middle two blocks are looped. Each pass incorporates Attention Residuals and a learned gate to pass information between iterations. The feed-forward layers utilize 128 experts, with 8 routed per token. During training, the model began with 384 experts per layer before pruning to 128, followed by a 1T-token distillation from a larger internal model. Benchmarks show a score of 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Index, tying it with Qwen3.8-27B, and a 79.2% success rate on SWE-bench Verified (bash only). However, the model exhibits limitations in knowledge recall and multi-turn instruction following, scoring 15.2% on HLE-Diamond and 50.0% on MultiChallenge.
takeaways: **Architecture Efficiency:** The model uses 3.4B active parameters per pass, reaching 5.4B effective parameters per token through looping, which provides a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain.
**Hardware Requirements:** The 20GB checkpoint is optimized for local deployment on systems with at least 32GB of VRAM or unified memory, with GGUF builds supported via Unsloth and llama.cpp.

**Training Methodology:** The model underwent a pruning process during mid-training, reducing expert count from 384 to 128, followed by distillation from a larger internal model to recover performance.

**Performance Metrics:** While the model excels in agentic coding tasks (79.2% on SWE-bench Verified), it shows weaker performance in general knowledge and multi-turn instruction following benchmarks.

title: OpenAI Ships GPT-Live-1.1 for Voice Agents, Cuts Idle Cost to $0.02/Min
author: Michal Sutter

Runs on: OpenAI’s cloud only, via v1/live/sessions . Clients connect over WebRTC or WebSocket. No open weights, no quantized variants. Performance: OpenAI claims better accents, transcription, letter and number handling, and task completion than GPT-Live-1. No scores published. Best: Standby bills idle WebRTC time at $0.02 per minute versus $0.05 active , a 60% lower rate. Worst: OpenAI published 0 benchmark scores for 1.1. Image, video and structured outputs are not supported. Bottom line: Best: cheaper always-on voice sessions. Worst: quality gains are self-reported with no numbers. What is GPT-Live-1.1? As per the OpenAI forum announcement , it has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. Inputs and outputs are audio and text. Image and video are not supported. Streaming and function calling work. Structured outputs, fine-tuning and predicted outputs do not. How does GPT-Live-1.1 work? The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model . It also handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Deeper work is delegated. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model. OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks. Third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses . Responses mode uses OpenAI models. Client mode connects your own backend. Instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. What changed from GPT-Live-1? O

summary.tldr:
OpenAI has released GPT-Live-1.1 (model ID: gpt-live-1.1), a full-duplex voice model designed for multilingual, real-time conversational agents. The model, which has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice features since October 15, 2026, replaces traditional cascaded speech-to-text and text-to-speech pipelines by reasoning over audio streams natively. It supports a 128,000-token context window and allows for function calling, though it lacks support for image, video, structured outputs, fine-tuning, or predicted outputs.

A primary commercial update in this release is the introduction of a 'standby' billing state for idle WebRTC sessions, which costs $0.02 per minute compared to the $0.05 per minute rate for active sessions, representing a 60% cost reduction for idle time. The model architecture supports native ASR transcript generation and allows developers to delegate complex reasoning or high-volume tasks to backend models such as GPT-6 Astra or Luna via the 'responses' or 'client' delegation modes. Instructions are limited to 16,384 tokens.

Despite the release, OpenAI has not published quantitative benchmark scores for GPT-Live-1.1, relying on self-reported improvements in accent consistency, transcription accuracy, and task completion reliability compared to the original GPT-Live-1. The model is available exclusively via OpenAI’s cloud API (v1/live/sessions) with no open weights or quantized variants provided.
takeaways: **Pricing:** Idle WebRTC sessions are billed at $0.02/min, a 60% reduction from the $0.05/min active session rate.
**Architecture:** The model uses a full-duplex, single-stream approach for audio input/output, bypassing traditional cascaded ASR/TTS pipelines.
**Context & Limits:** The model supports a 128,000-token context window and a 16,384-token limit for system instructions.
**Delegation:** Developers can route reasoning tasks to external backends like GPT-6 Astra or Luna using 'client' or 'responses' delegation modes.
**Compatibility:** The model supports WebRTC and WebSocket connections but excludes support for image, video, and structured output formats.

title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
author: Maohao Ran
contentSnippet: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.

title: When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
author: Feiyang Pan
contentSnippet: Large language models (LLMs) can generate register-transfer-level (RTL) designs from natural-language specifications. To improve functional correctness, many RTL agents use simulation feedback to guide refinement. However, without a reference testbench, generating one for every initial implementation incurs inference cost even when the RTL is correct. We therefore introduce an adaptive harness that uses a specialized decision model to orchestrate testing, refinement, and candidate selection. It accepts high-scoring initial implementations and generates testbenches for the rest. When further search is needed, the initial score guides repair--regeneration allocation, while defect rankings and simulation feedback guide repair. For final selection, the harness prioritizes test-passing candidates and ranks them using decision-model scores. Across three benchmarks, the harness with DeepSeek improves mean Pass@1 by 5.4--7.1 percentage points over initial implementations and reduces aggregate estimated inference cost by 11.0--14.3% relative to a testbench-guided repair baseline with the same candidate cap.

title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
author: Muxin Fu
contentSnippet: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
author: Xin Zhang
contentSnippet: Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets. We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K--64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65--0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28--23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08--1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.

Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step.

A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally.

The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets.
We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs.
